choices: Approve if unit tests cover the edge cases like empty values and fragments

Use an existing utility such as `net::QueryIterator`
Rewrite it with `std::regex` so the parsing is more robust to odd inputs

choices: Use `base::BindOnce` but pass the callback by `const&` to avoid a move
Nothing — `base::Bind` is fine as long as the callback runs only once
`base::OnceCallback` + `base::BindOnce`, passed via `std::move(cb)`
Replace it with a `std::function<void(bool)>` holding a lambda
explain: `base::Callback`/`base::Bind` are deprecated. Use `OnceCallback`/`BindOnce` (or the `Repeating` variants), and `std::move` a `OnceCallback` when passing or running it.

choices: Use `base::Time` / `base::TimeDelta` instead

Keep `time_t` but store it in a `uint64_t` to avoid the year-2038 problem
Fine — `std::time` is portable standard C++

choices: Keep the manual lookups; they're the most explicit and easiest to debug
Serialize with `JSONWriter` and pattern-match on the resulting string

prompt:
```cpp
std::unordered_map<std::string, double> feature_map_;
```

This is a general-purpose, unordered map of a few hundred entries. What should it be?
choices: `absl::btree_map<std::string, double>` for better cache behavior
It's fine — `std::unordered_map` is standard C++ and well understood
`std::map<std::string, double>`, since hash maps are banned in Chromium
`absl::flat_hash_map<std::string, double>`
explain: `std::unordered_map`/`set` are banned. Default to `absl::flat_hash_map`/`set`; `base::flat_map` for sorted small/write-once, `std::map` for large frequently-mutated sorted data. `absl::btree_*` is banned too.

prompt: You need a hash map where **pointers to keys** must stay valid while the map is mutated. Which container fits Chromium's guidelines?
choices: `absl::node_hash_map`
`base::flat_map`, wrapping each key in a `std::unique_ptr`
`absl::btree_map`, because tree nodes never move after insertion
`std::unordered_map`, since its nodes are separately allocated
explain: For key pointer stability use `absl::node_hash_map`/`node_hash_set`; for value stability, wrap values in `std::unique_ptr` inside an `absl::flat_hash_map`. `std::unordered_*` and `absl::btree_*` are banned.

choices: `const std::string& str = value->GetString();`
`base::JSONWriter::Write(*value, &str);`
`std::string str = value->DebugString();`
Keep it, but check the `bool` return value of `GetAsString()`
explain: `GetAsString()`, `GetAsInteger()` etc. on `base::Value` are deprecated. Use the direct accessors `GetString()`, `GetInt()`, `GetDouble()`.

choices: Use the older `value.GetAsBoolean(&b)` and check its return value
It's fine — `GetBool()` simply returns `false` on a type mismatch
`if (value.GetIfBool().value_or(false)) { ... }`
Wrap the call in `try { ... } catch (...)` to handle bad input
explain: `Get*()` CHECK-fails (crashes) on a type mismatch. When the type may differ, use `GetIfBool`/`GetIfInt`/`GetIfString`, typically with `.value_or(...)`.

`base::StringPrintf("%d", port)`

prompt:
```cpp
double ratio = (double)completed / total;  // both are int
```

explain: Chromium prohibits C-style casts. Use explicit C++ casts like `static_cast`, which are safer and searchable.

choices: It copies the whole vector; pass `std::move(buffer)`
None — the compiler elides the copy because `buffer` is a local
The callback should receive `buffer.data()` instead of the vector
Pass a clone explicitly so the ownership transfer is obvious to readers

Drop the wrapper and return `std::vector<MonthlyStatement>`
Keep it, but add a `using MonthlyStatementList = MonthlyStatements;` alias
Good — a named plural type documents intent better than a bare vector

choices: Split each key into its own separate string pref
As is — string prefs are the most portable and easiest to migrate
`prefs->SetDict(prefs::kMyPref, std::move(dict))` (or `SetList`)

prompt:

A global `const std::string kBraveSyncUrl` defined in the header

choices: An `enum class WalletType` parameter (with string conversion)

Keep the string but `DCHECK` that it's one of the allowed values

prompt: You're integrating a third-party C++ library whose code uses `throw` and `try/catch` for error handling. What must you verify?

That it builds with exception support disabled
That every call into it from Brave code is wrapped in `try/catch`
That exceptions never propagate past the library's public API boundary

choices: Copy the non-expired entries into a new `flat_set` and swap

prompt:
```cpp
void ProcessBuffer(const std::vector<uint8_t>& data);  // read-only
```

Callers hold data in `std::vector`, `base::HeapArray`, and static arrays. Best signature?
choices: `void ProcessBuffer(const uint8_t* data, size_t size);`
`template <typename C> void ProcessBuffer(const C& data);`
Keep `const std::vector<uint8_t>&` and convert at each call site
`void ProcessBuffer(base::span<const uint8_t> data);`
explain: Use `base::span<const T>` for read-only parameters — a lightweight non-owning view that accepts any contiguous container.

prompt:
```cpp
std::vector<int> scores(num_players);  // num_players known at runtime
// scores is filled in but never resized
```

What container best communicates the intent?
choices: `std::array<int, kMaxPlayers>` sized to the largest possible value
`base::FixedArray<int> scores(num_players);`
`std::list<int>` so elements never need reallocation
`std::vector<int>` with a `reserve(num_players)` call
explain: When size is known at creation but not at compile time, `base::FixedArray` communicates the fixed size and avoids heap allocation for small sizes.

choices: `auto buf = base::HeapArray<uint8_t>::WithSize(size); ProcessBuffer(buf.as_span());`
`auto buf = std::make_unique<uint8_t[]>(size); ProcessBuffer(buf.get(), size);`
`std::vector<uint8_t> buf; buf.reserve(size); ProcessBuffer(buf.data(), size);`
`std::string buf(size, '\0'); ProcessBuffer(buf.data(), buf.size());`
explain: Use `base::HeapArray<uint8_t>` for fixed-size owned byte buffers: fixed-size semantics, bounds-checked indexing, easy `base::span` conversion. `Uninit(size)` skips zero-init on hot paths.

choices: `std::vector<std::string> names(items.begin(), items.end());`

prompt: A class stores `std::list<Entry> entries_;`. Entries are appended once, then only iterated front-to-back. What should the reviewer suggest?

Use `std::set<Entry>` so iteration order is deterministic
Switch to `std::forward_list` to save one pointer per node

choices: Use a reserved value like `"__unset__"` so empty titles are allowed

`void SetCustomTitle(std::optional<std::string> title);`

`elapsed_timer_ = std::make_optional<base::ElapsedTimer>();`
`elapsed_timer_.emplace();`
